Building a Competitive Intelligence Engine at SAP Concur

Lauren Cochrane is leading the rollout of Crayon and piloting Clozd — creating a centralized competitive intelligence and win-loss system.

By Chris O'Hara · April 15, 2026 · 12 min read

If you want to know what it actually takes to bring new competitive intelligence tools into SAP, Lauren Cochrane is living the journey right now — and she's sharing the lessons along the way.

Lauren is leading the rollout of Crayon for competitive intelligence and piloting Clozd for win-loss analysis at SAP Concur. The goal? An AI-driven centralized competitive intelligence engine that serves sales, marketing, and product teams — turning fragmented insights into systematic and scalable advantage.

The work is ongoing, and Lauren is navigating the realities of enterprise vendor onboarding in real-time — a process that anyone who's worked in large organizations knows can be challenging.

That candor makes her insights even more valuable. For the rest of us looking to bring similar tools into our teams, Lauren's experience is a live roadmap — complete with warning signs and early wins.

The Tools: Crayon + Clozd

🖍️

Crayon

Competitive Intelligence Platform
Automated tracking, battlecards, and insights delivery. Monitors competitor moves across web, news, reviews, and more.

🎯

Clozd

Win-Loss Analysis
Structured buyer interviews and analysis to understand why deals are won or lost — direct from the decision-makers themselves.

Together, these tools will give SAP Concur two complementary views: what competitors are doing (Crayon) and what buyers actually think (Clozd). The combination is powerful — competitive intelligence grounded in real deal outcomes.

Note: Clozd is currently being piloted with procurement approval for this year. Later this year, CMI will open an RFP to evaluate the current win-loss program.

The Vision: What Success Looks Like

Lauren's vision for where this is heading is worth quoting in full, because it shows how competitive intelligence should extend beyond just the compete team:

"The Compete and extended product marketing teams use a centralized competitive intelligence engine to efficiently analyze and share insights with stakeholders across the business."
— Lauren Cochrane

Here's what she's building toward — the downstream effects that will make this investment pay off:

💰

Sales Adoption

Greater awareness and proficiency against strategic competitors → higher competitive win rates

📢

Marketing Adoption

Faster iteration on positioning, messaging, and tactics → improved pipeline vs. competitors

🛠️

Product Adoption

Informs product strategy and priorities → keep pace with nimble competitors and differentiate

This is the right way to think about competitive intelligence tools: not as a PMM silo, but as infrastructure that serves the entire go-to-market engine.

The Engine in Action: From Signals to Field Enablement

What does this look like in practice? Lauren recently presented to the SAP Concur sales community, showing how the "Compete Insights Engine" turns raw market signals into actionable field enablement. The framework makes the value chain concrete:

🔄 Compete Insights Engine — Signal to Action

Inputs

  • Salesforce Deal Data — what's happening
  • Voice of Field — seller perspective
  • Voice of Buyer — buyer truth (via Clozd)
→

Outputs

  • Insights for Sales — battlecards, alerts
  • Product Priorities — roadmap influence
  • Positioning & Messaging — marketing fuel
  • Leadership Influence — strategic decisions

Powered by Crayon++ with Clozd integration

The outputs aren't theoretical — they're already being produced. Here's the content matrix being built by the Compete team in partnership with Marketing:

Asset Type Status Competitors Covered
Battlecards ✅ Live Navan, Coupa, Emburse, Ramp, Oracle, Workday
Head-to-Head Blogs ✅ Live Navan, Coupa, Oracle
Head-to-Head Landing Pages ✅ Live Expensify, Coupa, Navan, Workday, Ramp, Oracle
BOFU eBooks ✅ Navan live, more coming Navan + expansion planned
Displacement Guides 🔜 Coming Navan, Coupa, Workday, Oracle, Emburse, Ramp
Win-Loss QuickViews ✅ Live (US) All strategic competitors
Compete Alerts ✅ Live Real-time via Crayon

This is what "competitive intelligence as infrastructure" looks like: a systematic content engine that produces battlecards, landing pages, eBooks, and displacement guides — all grounded in deal data and buyer feedback. The content lives in a Highspot hub ("Competitive Takedown Hub") so sales can access everything in context.

The competitors getting the most attention? Emburse, Ramp, Navan, and Oracle — the players that are "louder, bolder, and increasingly naming SAP directly," as Lauren put it to the sales team. That's the market reality driving the investment.

The SAP Vendor Reality

Lauren's honest assessment of the onboarding process is a useful heads-up for anyone considering similar tools:

⚠️ Bringing New Vendors into SAP: The Reality

  • Procurement complexity — expect multiple rounds of review
  • Security and compliance — particularly for any data and AI tools
  • Integration requirements — connecting to existing systems takes time
  • Change management — getting teams to actually adopt new tools

The complexity isn't unique to these vendors — it's the reality of enterprise procurement at scale. What matters is whether the payoff justifies the effort. For Lauren's team, it clearly will.

The Current State: What They're Replacing

Lauren's evaluation didn't happen in a vacuum. The Concur Compete team was already using tools that weren't meeting expectations — and lacked the automation and AI capabilities needed to scale. Here's what they were working with:

🔴 Valona (Competitive News Tracking) — Pain Points

  • Restrictive commercial model: Commercial model restricts the number of competitors tracked — research platform and AI agents additional cost
  • Manual-heavy processes: Platform reliant on manual processes, not automated enough, with limited use cases
  • Narrow content focus: Coverage limited to news only — no broader competitive intelligence

🔴 Anova (Win-Loss) — Pain Points

  • Falling short of expectations: Program not delivering the insights needed
  • Lack of automation: Manual processes that don't scale
  • Missing AI capabilities: No modern AI-powered analysis
  • No interview recordings: Interviews aren't recorded, limiting ability to revisit and extract additional insights
  • Limited global expertise: Lack of international experience and reach for global win-loss programs

The pattern is clear: manual processes, limited coverage, outdated content cycles, and lack of integration or real-time insights. This is the reality at many enterprise compete teams — and why Lauren's evaluation matters beyond just SAP Concur.

The Evaluation: Why Crayon + Clozd Won

Lauren evaluated three primary vendors: Crayon, Clozd, and Klue (which offers both CI and win-loss in one platform). Here's how they stacked up:

🖍️ Crayon — Recommended for Competitive Intelligence

✅ Why Crayon Won

  • AI-Powered Research Agent: Modern AI that allows users to ask specific questions and receive immediate, tailored insights
  • Cost-Effective Pricing: Based on number of tracked competitors, not user count — more scalable
  • Strong Integrations: Seamless connections with CRM, Teams, Clozd, and MCP
  • Consultative Account Management: High-touch support model

🎯 Clozd — Recommended for Win-Loss

✅ Why Clozd Won

  • Cost-Efficient Interview Model: Commercial structure allows higher volume of interviews at lower cost, with flexible timing
  • Native Multilingual Capabilities: Non-English interviews conducted by trained Clozd employees — no external translators needed
  • Global Platform Access Controls: Role-based access for compliance with data privacy regulations
  • Robust Integrations: Seamless Salesforce and Crayon integration for data flow
  • Automated Outreach: Highly customizable workflows streamline scheduling and follow-ups at scale
  • Exceptional Account Experience: Strong marks from industry professionals for high-touch engagement

🔄 Klue — Why We Chose Differently

Considerations That Informed Our Decision

  • Pricing model: Based on 3,000 provisioned users — different scalability tradeoffs
  • No interview carryovers: Unused interviews don't roll over
  • +$500 per non-English interview: Higher surcharge for global programs
  • All-in-one vs. best-of-breed: We decided the specialist approach better fit our needs

The lesson here: best-of-breed often beats all-in-one. Crayon and Clozd each excel at their core function, and the integration between them (Clozd has native Crayon integration) creates a more powerful combined solution than a single platform trying to do both.

Pricing Transparency

One of the most valuable aspects of Lauren's evaluation is the pricing transparency. Here's how the costs compare:

Vendor Category Pricing Model
Valona (current) Competitive Intelligence Based on # of competitors
Crayon ✅ Competitive Intelligence Based on # of PRO competitors (10 Pro + unlimited Standard); unlimited users, battlecards, newsletters, AI queries, integrations
Clozd ✅ Win-Loss Based on 20 annual interviews; +$300/non-English interview (Spanish, Portuguese, German, French, Italian, Korean, Japanese)
Klue CI + Win-Loss Based on 3,000 provisioned users; no interview carryovers; +$500/non-English interview

The key insight: Crayon's unlimited user model scales better for large organizations, and Clozd's native multilingual support ($300 vs. $500 for non-English) makes global win-loss programs more affordable.

Early Lessons for the Broader SAP PMM Community

Even in the early stages, Lauren's experience is already surfacing patterns that matter for anyone considering similar tools:

✅ What's Working So Far

  • Two tools, complementary purposes — CI tracking + win-loss analysis gives complete picture
  • Centralized engine approach — one source of truth, multiple consumers
  • Cross-functional adoption goals — designed for sales, marketing, AND product from the start
  • Clear success metrics — tied to win rates, pipeline, and product priorities

The key insight emerging: don't think of competitive intelligence as a tool for the compete team. Think of it as infrastructure for go-to-market excellence.

How Other Teams Can Learn

If you're considering Crayon, Clozd, or similar tools for your team, here's the practical guidance based on Lauren's experience:

  1. Start with the outcome, not the tool — What decisions will this enable? What metrics will improve?
  2. Plan for procurement friction — Build in extra time for security reviews and approvals
  3. Design for multiple stakeholders — Sales, marketing, and product should all see value from day one
  4. Define your "centralized engine" — Where will insights live? How will they flow?
  5. Measure adoption, not just deployment — The tool is only valuable if people use it

The Bigger Picture

Lauren's work at SAP Concur is exactly the kind of operational excellence we need more of across SAP. Rather than relying on ad-hoc competitive research or tribal knowledge locked in individual heads, she's building systematic infrastructure that scales.

That's the shift she's driving: from competitive intelligence as occasional project to competitive intelligence as always-on capability.

For those of us thinking about AI tools and automation, this is also a reminder: sometimes the right answer isn't building something custom. It's selecting, evaluating, and implementing best-in-class vendors — then driving adoption across the org. We'll continue to follow Lauren's progress and share updates as this rollout matures.
